question: A 58-year-old man is found to have IOP 26 mmHg on routine testing. Which combination of additional findings would confirm a diagnosis of primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG)?

answers.text: Shallow anterior chamber on slit-lamp and positive van Herick grade I

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A shallow anterior chamber with van Herick grade I suggests angle-closure disease (PACG risk), not POAG. In POAG the angle is open — gonioscopy shows a wide open angle bilaterally.

answers.text: Cup-to-disc ratio 0.8 with inferior neuroretinal rim thinning and inferior arcuate scotoma on visual fields, with open angle on gonioscopy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. POAG diagnosis requires the triad: glaucomatous optic nerve changes (large C:D, ISNT rule violation, NRR thinning), corresponding visual field defects, AND an open angle on gonioscopy — all in the absence of a secondary cause.

answers.text: IOP 26 mmHg with a normal disc and normal visual fields

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes ocular hypertension (OHT), not POAG. POAG requires evidence of glaucomatous optic nerve damage and/or visual field loss — raised IOP alone is insufficient.

answers.text: Diffuse corneal oedema, mid-dilated pupil, and IOP 52 mmHg

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This clinical picture — acutely elevated IOP with corneal oedema and mid-dilated pupil — is characteristic of acute primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG), not POAG, which is a chronic, asymptomatic condition.

overallFeedback.feedback: POAG requires three elements confirmed: open iridocorneal angle on gonioscopy, glaucomatous optic nerve damage (large C:D, ISNT violation, NRR thinning), and matching visual field defects.
Excellent. The POAG triad: open angle (gonioscopy), glaucomatous optic nerve changes, and corresponding visual field loss — plus ruling out secondary causes.
